frameworks.name: Diagnostic Sales Process
frameworks.definition: A 7-8 step sales framework that replaces transactional one-off selling with a goal-anchored, personalized presentation: pre-sale questionnaire, credit card collection, current state elicitation, desired state elicitation, obstacle identification, price presentation tied to the goal, prepayment incentive, and recurring/continuity transition.

frameworks.name: Sales Step-Downs
frameworks.definition: A cascading offer sequence presented after the goal-price is established: (1) prepay in full for largest discount, (2) third-party financing, (3) partial payment with smaller discount, (4) payment plan continuity, (5) book next appointment — ensuring every customer buys something.

frameworks.name: Transactional vs. Custom Sale Spectrum
frameworks.definition: A two-pole model of sales: transactional (high velocity, low ticket, customer fit to product) vs. enterprise/relational (custom, high touch, stakeholder-driven); the diagnostic sale occupies the profitable middle by delivering a product-level operation while feeling custom to the buyer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that after installing a diagnostic sales process into a brick-and-mortar chain they acquired (approximately 14 locations at time of purchase, ca. 2022-2023), average revenue per customer rose from $200 to $800 without changing the underlying service delivered — a 4x increase in lifetime value progression driven solely by repackaging how the service was presented and sold.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brick-and-mortar chain service business
existing strong lead generation already in place
offer constraint identified via secret shop
claims.mechanism: The new process sold to the customer's goal (desired outcome) rather than selling a transactional service, which justified a larger committed purchase.
bounded_by: Business already had strong lead generation; process improvement alone would not compensate for weak demand
Required management team buy-in and full implementation across all locations

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that after implementing the diagnostic sales process in the same acquired chain, recurring revenue as a share of the product line rose from 9% to 60%, and membership penetration went from near zero to 30%, while average visits per customer rose from approximately 2 to 4-6 and the product line's monthly revenue grew from $20,000 to over $250,000.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: single product line within a multi-service brick-and-mortar chain
full diagnostic process implementation including recurring/continuity step
claims.mechanism: By introducing goal-anchored packages and a continuity payment structure at the close, customers committed to longer programs rather than one-off transactions.

numbers.axis: key business metrics before vs. after diagnostic process

anchors.region: recurring revenue % of product line — before
recurring revenue % of product line — after

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in any sales conversation, raising objections or counter-arguments after the price has been revealed is far less effective than addressing them before, because once a price is stated the buyer perceives the salesperson as adversarial and discounts any subsequent explanation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: face-to-face or phone sales where price is stated explicitly
claims.mechanism: Once a price is disclosed, the buyer frames all seller communication as motivated by self-interest (commission/close), reducing persuasive weight of subsequent objection handling.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that winning an argument with a prospect during a sales conversation causes the sale to be lost, because the buyer who is made to feel wrong about their objection will not buy from someone who defeated them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales conversation with an undecided prospect
claims.mechanism: Being made to feel wrong triggers defensive identity protection; the buyer redirects energy from evaluating the offer to winning the interpersonal contest.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for upsell offers to materially increase average transaction value, the upsell price must be approximately 5x the core offer price, because if 20% of buyers take the upsell (the approximate top-spending quintile), the revenue math only becomes significant when the upsell is 5x the original ticket.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brick-and-mortar or service business with a defined core offer price
claims.mechanism: The top 20% of customers by spending have approximately 5x the spending power of the bottom 80%; an upsell priced at 5x the core offer, taken by 20% of buyers, doubles the average ticket.

numbers.axis: upsell price as multiple of core offer, impact on average ticket

anchors.region: upsell at 10% of core offer (e.g., $100 on $1,000 base)
anchors.value: avg ticket moves from $1,000 to $1,020 if 20% take it — negligible

anchors.region: upsell at 5x core offer (e.g., $5,000 on $1,000 base)
anchors.value: avg ticket moves from $1,000 to $2,000 if 20% take it — doubles average ticket

bounded_by: Requires the top spending quintile to genuinely have 5x spending power relative to the mean buyer — may not hold in commodity or low-income markets

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends presenting the highest (full payment-plan) price first and then offering prepayment discounts, rather than anchoring to the discounted price and adding financing surcharges, because the former frames the seller as the generous party who is giving the buyer a benefit, while the latter frames the seller as penalizing buyers who cannot pay upfront.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales contexts where multiple payment structures are available (prepay, partial, payment plan)
claims.mechanism: Anchoring high and discounting down triggers the buyer's gain framing (receiving a benefit); anchoring low and surcharging up triggers loss framing (paying a penalty), which increases resistance.

numbers.axis: price presentation sequence and buyer psychology

anchors.value: $4,500 — buyer then shown savings of $900 (20%) for prepay = $3,600

anchors.region: discounted price presented first then surcharge added
anchors.value: $3,600 anchor; buyer then told they owe 25% more if they cannot pay upfront

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that selling to the customer's desired outcome (goal) rather than to the service features produces a significantly higher per-customer price, because the customer evaluates the purchase as the cost of achieving the outcome — making an outcome-priced offer more defensible than a feature-priced one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses where the customer has a measurable goal (weight, aesthetics, painting completion, etc.)
business is delivering the same underlying service regardless of framing
claims.mechanism: When price is anchored to the total cost of achieving the buyer's stated goal (e.g., $4,500 to lose 60 lbs over 45 weeks), the buyer evaluates it against the value of the goal, not the cost per session — removing the per-unit pricing comparison.
bounded_by: Requires that a measurable, quantifiable goal can be established in the conversation
Does not apply to transactional or commodity purchases where the buyer has no specific outcome target

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that allowing the customer to self-identify their current state and desired outcome — rather than having the salesperson diagnose them — increases customer commitment to the resulting price, because the goal and therefore the price originated from the customer's own statements.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sales conversation where a measurable current state and desired state can be elicited
claims.mechanism: When a buyer states their own goal, they experience ownership of that goal; the resulting price (derived from their goal) is harder for them to reject without implicitly rejecting their own stated aspiration.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that a friend's membership business converted the same $300/month offer from month-to-month billing to a $10,000 program with 36 months of interest-free financing, which increased average customer tenure from 3 months to 8 months without changing the service, raising average revenue per customer from $900 to $2,400.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: membership or recurring service business
offer and price point remain identical in total value
claims.mechanism: Buyers who commit to a large fixed program (payment plan structure) are psychologically more resistant to cancellation than month-to-month subscribers, because canceling breaks a commitment they consciously made rather than simply failing to renew.

numbers.axis: billing structure impact on customer tenure and revenue

bounded_by: Service quality and delivery must remain constant; this restructuring only affects payment commitment, not satisfaction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customers are significantly less likely to churn out of a payment plan than out of a month-to-month recurring revenue subscription, even when the monthly dollar amount is identical.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses with recurring delivery
claims.mechanism: A payment plan creates an upfront psychological commitment to a defined program; canceling it requires breaking a contract the buyer entered intentionally. Month-to-month subscriptions require only passive non-renewal — no active commitment is broken.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that collecting a credit card during the account setup step — before any offer is made — removes the friction of asking for payment information at the close, which otherwise can break momentum or cause buyers to pause and reconsider.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: in-person or phone sales with a defined close step
business has a customer account profile or registration process
claims.mechanism: Asking for a credit card mid-conversation interrupts the emotional close; collecting it earlier under a neutral framing (account setup) normalizes card surrender and allows the close to proceed directly to confirmation.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that in low-skill, brick-and-mortar sales environments, the quality of sales execution is determined primarily by how simple the process is made for frontline staff, not by their inherent sales ability, because simpler scripts have higher adherence rates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brick-and-mortar chain with hourly or low-wage frontline staff
sales team is not professionally trained salespeople
claims.mechanism: Low-skill labor retains and executes only simple, repeatable scripts; adding complexity reduces adherence, so the limiting factor is script simplicity, not staff capability.
bounded_by: Does not apply to high-ticket enterprise or relational sales where customization is required

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the transactional sale (fitting the customer to a fixed product) is operationally efficient but economically constrained, while the custom/diagnostic sale is operationally harder but unlocks significantly higher per-customer revenue — and the optimal position is to operate with transactional delivery while creating a custom-feeling sales experience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses that deliver a standardized core service (fitness, aesthetics, HVAC, painting)
claims.mechanism: Standardized delivery keeps operational costs low; a diagnostic sales experience increases perceived personalization and willingness to pay, capturing the economic upside of custom sales without the delivery complexity.
bounded_by: Requires the service to have a definable goal that can be elicited from the customer
Does not apply to pure commodity goods where the product is undifferentiated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that the pre-sale questionnaire serves a dual purpose: it gathers information that arms the salesperson, and simultaneously agitates the buyer's awareness of their own problem by asking the same pain question multiple ways (cost today, cost over five years) — elevating urgency before the sales conversation begins.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses with a defined intake or appointment process
claims.mechanism: Quantifying pain in monetary terms (what has this cost you financially, what would five more years cost) forces the buyer to self-calculate the cost of inaction, raising the perceived value of a solution before price is mentioned.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that tying a money-back guarantee to the customer's own compliance (show up, log food, follow steps) rather than unconditionally removes financial risk for the seller while maintaining the psychological value of the guarantee for the buyer, since most buyers who intend to comply will accept the condition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses where customer compliance is the primary determinant of outcome
goal-anchored sales where a specific outcome is promised
claims.mechanism: A compliance-conditioned guarantee shifts outcome risk back to the buyer (who controls compliance) while preserving the closing power of a guarantee. Buyers who plan to comply view this as essentially unconditional.
bounded_by: Does not apply to services where outcome is entirely within the provider's control (product delivery, painting)

examples.text: Alex Hormozi illustrates the diagnostic sales process using a weight-loss gym scenario. A customer walks in at 200 lbs wanting to reach 140 lbs. Rather than selling a $99/month membership, Hormozi has the salesperson calculate: 60 lbs to lose at 1.5 lbs/week = 45 weeks. At $99/week, that is $4,500 total. The salesperson says: 'When you pay this $4,500, you can count that weight gone for good — I'll keep working with you for free until you get there, as long as you follow the steps.' The buyer is then offered a 10% prepayment discount ($450 off) using the card already on file. The sale thus moved from a $99/month membership to a $4,500 goal-anchored program, using the same service.

Alex Hormozi illustrates self-identification of desired state using an aesthetics/filler business. Instead of diagnosing how unattractive the customer is, the salesperson shows a chart of faces at various filler densities and asks the customer to pick where they currently see themselves, then where they want to be. The customer sets their own goal. Hormozi draws the parallel to yogurt stores where the customer fills their own cup and then sees the weight on the scale — they feel responsible for the quantity and price, not the business. In the same way, the aesthetics customer who chose their target look cannot object to a price derived from their own stated goal.

Alex Hormozi describes a friend whose membership business was stuck at 3-month average LTV at $300/month ($900 per customer). The friend restructured the same $300/month service as a $10,000 program with 36 months of interest-free financing. Nothing about the service changed. Average customer tenure went from 3 months to 8 months, raising revenue per customer from $900 to $2,400 — a 2.7x improvement in revenue per customer with zero change to what was delivered.

Alex Hormozi describes the secret shop of the acquired brick-and-mortar chain before completing the investment. His sales director visited as a customer and found: no pre-sale questionnaire, no credit card or information collection before service, a partial current-state identification (how ugly are you on this scale) but no desired-state question, no package or program offer at close, just payment for one session, and a single low-value upsell of approximately $20 on a $200 average customer. Hormozi used these gaps as the acquisition thesis — each missing step was a lever that, once added, would compound to multiply recurring revenue.

Alex Hormozi contrasts two price-presentation sequences using the same 45-week weight-loss program example. In the first (recommended) version, the salesperson presents the full payment-plan price of $4,500, then offers a $900 (20%) saving for prepaying, dropping to $3,600, or $450 (10%) for half-down at $4,050. The buyer feels they are receiving a benefit. In the second (common mistake) version, the salesperson anchors at $3,600 and then reveals financing adds 10-20% interest — the buyer who cannot pay upfront now faces a higher number than the anchor, creating the same emotional dynamic as a bank penalty, which Hormozi notes universally generates negative feeling.

practices.text: Secret shop your own business before assuming the sales script is being followed; Hormozi recommends doing it because the gap between what owners believe is happening and what frontline staff actually say is typically severe.

When handling objections after a price is stated, use a head-tilt and childlike curiosity framing (e.g., 'huh, that's interesting — what changed between then and now?') rather than a counter-argument, to keep the buyer in explanation mode rather than defensive mode.

Train sales staff to say 'prepayment discount' not 'paid in full' — the former is a customer benefit framing, the latter is a salesperson's internal accounting term that sounds transactional to the buyer.

Build point-of-sale automation checkboxes that force script steps to be completed before staff can advance in the system, so that script adherence is structurally enforced rather than relying on memory.

Install the mantra 'everyone buys something' within a sales team to ensure that every customer interaction ends with at least the lowest step-down offer (rebook next appointment) rather than walking out with no purchase.

When transitioning a payment plan to recurring, automatically attach the recurring charge at the same price as the payment plan installment at the end of the program, so the continuity feels like a natural extension rather than a new sale.

Apply the diagnostic sales framework across radically different service verticals by identifying the current state, desired state, and obstacle for whatever the customer truly wants — the underlying goal, not the service feature they named (e.g., buyers of house painting want a fully weatherproofed house by a deadline, not 'four coats of paint').
